opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a very formative period for me, even though it ended up pointing me in a different direction.

When I first arrived at Stanford, I was working on semiconductor fabrication. That meant a lot of time in the cleanroom: wearing the bunny suit, running the process steps, waiting for results. One thing I learned very quickly is how slow the iteration cycle is in that field. You design something, you go through dozens of process steps, and weeks later you find out whether it worked. Very often it didn't, and sometimes you couldn't even tell exactly why. It trained my patience and my rigor, and I really respect people who devote their careers to it. But I started to feel that the feedback loop didn't fit how I like to think and explore.

At the same time, around 2015 and 2016, deep learning was taking off. Everyone at Stanford could feel it. You'd walk around campus and people were talking about ImageNet, about AlphaGo, about what neural networks could suddenly do. I took some courses and started playing with code, and the contrast was striking. In AI you could have an idea in the morning, implement it in the afternoon, and see results that night. That speed of iteration was very attractive to me.

There was also a deeper reason. In semiconductors, a lot of the big direction is already set by the industry roadmap; progress is incremental and very capital-intensive. In AI, it felt like the fundamental questions were still wide open. How do machines perceive the 3D world? How do they understand objects and interact with them? Those felt like questions where a young researcher could still make a real contribution.

So I made the switch and moved into computer vision and 3D understanding. Looking back, the fabrication experience wasn't wasted at all. It gave me a respect for the physical world, for hardware, for how hard it is to make real things work reliably. That turned out to matter a lot later, when I moved toward robotics and embodied intelligence. In the end, AI has to come back to the physical world, and having spent time in the cleanroom, I never forgot how unforgiving the physical world can be.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts slow fabrication cycles with the way He Wang likes to think and explore, but it does not identify a preference for mathematical modeling.

r002.rationale: It says fabrication could take weeks to reveal results, while in AI he could have an idea in the morning, implement it in the afternoon, and see results that night.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a good question, because at the time it didn't feel like a decision at all. It felt more like a slow realization.

When I was at Stanford I spent a lot of time in the cleanroom. And the cleanroom teaches you a certain kind of patience. You're doing lithography, deposition, etching, and a single run can take days. If something goes wrong at step twelve, you often don't find out until step twenty, and then you go back and start over. I actually loved that discipline. It makes you very careful about process, about how one small variable propagates through everything downstream.

But two things happened. The first was that I started to notice where the real bottleneck was. We were pushing transistors smaller and smaller, and the physics was getting harder, the costs were getting enormous, and the gains per generation were shrinking. Meanwhile, on the other side of the campus, people were showing that if you just took existing hardware and organized the computation differently, you could get results that looked almost like a new kind of capability, not just a faster version of the old one. That asymmetry stuck with me. Hardware progress was becoming incremental, and the software layer on top of it was suddenly behaving in a very nonlinear way.

The second thing was more personal. In fabrication, the feedback loop is very long. In machine learning, I could have an idea in the morning, write it, train it, and by the evening know whether I was wrong. For someone who likes to think by experimenting, that speed was intoxicating. I realized I was spending my evenings reading papers that had nothing to do with my thesis.

What I want to say, though, is that the semiconductor background didn't get thrown away. It shaped how I think about AI quite a lot. I think of models the way I used to think about a process flow: there's a yield, there are defects, there are variables you can't fully observe, and the thing you build is only as good as your ability to measure it. A lot of people come to AI from pure math or pure software, and they're surprised by how much of it is messy, empirical, almost like a manufacturing problem. For me that part felt very familiar.

And honestly, now that compute has become the scarcest resource in the field, I find myself coming back to that world. The chip and the model are no longer separate questions. So in a way the switch was less of a departure and more of a loop.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes fabrication as careful, process-oriented work and says he preferred rapid experimentation. It does not identify a preference for mathematical modeling or a mismatch with fabrication’s trial-and-error emphasis.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts fabrication’s very long feedback loop with being able to conceive an idea, test it, and know by evening whether it worked in machine learning.

astra-6.text:
Working on semiconductor fabrication at Stanford made me think about how much progress depends on the speed of experimentation. You have an idea, but getting to a result involves a lot of physical steps, and each iteration takes time. I appreciated the rigor of that process, but I also found myself drawn to questions I could explore through computation.

AI was appealing because you could try an idea, see where it failed, and use that feedback to shape the next experiment. That didn’t make the problems easier, but it made the process of exploring them exciting to me. So the shift was less about losing interest in semiconductors and more about discovering the kind of research I wanted to spend my time doing.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts slow physical fabrication with computational exploration, but it does not mention a preference for mathematical modeling.

sol-6.1.text: Working on semiconductor fabrication at Stanford helped me understand what kind of work I enjoyed. Fabrication involves a lot of careful experimentation, but the feedback loop can be slow—you make a change, go through the process, and then find out whether it worked. I found myself drawn to problems where I could test ideas and iterate more quickly. AI offered that, along with the opportunity to work on how machines perceive and interact with the world. So I see the switch as a continuation of my interest in building things, but at a different level.
